title: Further Concepts in Ethnicity
summary: How ethnic and group consciousness form, ethnicity as a social theory, and the debate over ethnicity and intelligence testing.

lesson.title: Why strangers abroad become kin
lesson.hook: Two Nigerians who would never greet each other in Lagos may hug like siblings when they meet in London. What turns 'not my people' into 'my people' the moment you leave home?

slides.heading: Ethnic consciousness starts early
slides.body:
Children are thought to begin noticing ethnic differences around **age 3 or 4**. At first this is simple awareness: 'we speak this way, they speak that way'.

In this session, **ethnic consciousness** means a person's awareness of belonging to an ethnic group. But scholars such as McCall (1955) and Kasfir (1979) stress that it goes beyond awareness. It shows up in **concrete action**: whom you choose as friends, partners, business allies or political candidates.

slides.heading: Why it is so visible in Nigeria
slides.body:
Nigeria has three large groups, the **Hausa-Fulani, Yoruba and Igbo**, and roughly 250 smaller groups. Modern cities such as Lagos, Kano and Port Harcourt grew by drawing migrants from everywhere.

When many groups suddenly share streets, markets and jobs, people notice difference more, and they lean on ethnic networks for housing, credit and protection. That is why ethnic consciousness in Nigerian cities is hard to overstate.

slides.question: According to Kasfir and McCall, ethnic consciousness is more than awareness because it:
options: Shows itself in deliberate affiliations and actions
slides.why: These scholars argue that ethnic consciousness turns into concrete choices of association. Skin colour points to race, not ethnic consciousness.

terms.meaning: Also used for the group consciousness that excluded or subordinated groups express
A shared heritage: ancestry, origin myths, homeland, language, religion, cuisine, dress, art
Members' awareness of the group, its people and what they have in common

slides.heading: Ethnicity as a social theory
slides.body:
As a **social theory**, ethnicity rejects the idea that the **physical body** explains why people differ. It argues against the claim that conflicts between groups are permanent because they spring from unchangeable physical differences.

**Ethnic theory** both describes how intergroup conflicts arise and prescribes ways of overcoming them. Those remedies were applied to racial exclusion between white and non-white people.

slides.heading: An unintended twist
slides.body:
There is an irony examiners like. In the United States, applying ethnic theory to race sometimes **reformulated and reinforced** the white-black divide instead of dissolving it.

Why? European immigrant groups were treated as 'ethnic' groups who could blend in over time, while Black Americans were still seen through the lens of race. So a theory meant to downplay the body ended up drawing a sharper line between the two categories.

slides.question: Which statement best captures ethnicity as a social theory?
options: Group differences come from fixed physical traits
Conflicts between groups can never be resolved
Differences between people are social and can be addressed
slides.why: Ethnic theory rejects body-based explanations and prescribes ways of overcoming conflict. The first two options describe the very view it argues against.

slides.heading: How group consciousness forms abroad
slides.body:
**Group consciousness** is to a group what self-consciousness is to a person: awareness of 'us'. It often becomes sharpest when migrants are **excluded by their host society**.

People who at home identified with a village or clan begin to feel close to anyone from the same country or region. Being lumped together by outsiders, plus a new sense of being 'from the same place', makes them see each other as compatriots.

slides.heading: Sabo in Ibadan
slides.story: Hausa traders who settled in Ibadan built the Sabo quarter, a community with its own mosques, leaders and trade in cattle and kola. Back home, these traders came from different towns and families. In Ibadan they became one community: they housed newcomers, shared trade information and settled disputes among themselves. The anthropologist Abner Cohen (1969) studied how this ethnic network protected their long-distance trade.
slides.takeaway: Commonality in a strange land creates trade networks, enclaves and institutions, not just nostalgia.

steps.title: Exclusion
steps.detail: Hostility or nativism from the host society

steps.title: Wider solidarity
steps.detail: Village ties widen into regional or national ties

steps.title: Networks
steps.detail: Trade, credit and social links form

steps.title: Nostalgia
steps.detail: Shared longing for home binds people

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: A favourite is an EXCEPT question listing factors that create group consciousness, with one odd option such as 'controlling extraneous differences', which belongs to intelligence testing. Another trap: thinking group consciousness abroad is only a reaction to hostility. It also builds trade networks and institutions.
slides.sampleQuestion: Explain how group consciousness is formed among migrants, using a named Nigerian example.
slides.howToAnswer: Define group consciousness, then list exclusion, widened solidarity, networks of trade, enclaves and nostalgia. Illustrate with the Hausa Sabo quarters in southern cities.

points: Ethnic awareness is thought to begin around age 3 or 4.
Ethnic consciousness moves from awareness to deliberate affiliation.
Ethnic theory rejects body-based explanations and prescribes remedies.
In the US it ironically reinforced the white-black distinction.
Exclusion abroad creates solidarity, networks, enclaves and institutions.

questions.stem: From a developmental view, children are often said to begin noticing their ethnicity at about age:
questions.explanation: Awareness of ethnic difference is commonly placed around 3 to 4 years. By adolescence it is already well established, so the later ages are too late.

questions.stem: Which three groups are usually described as Nigeria's dominant ethnic groups?
questions.explanation: The Hausa-Fulani, Yoruba and Igbo are the three largest groups. The others named are among the roughly 250 smaller groups.

questions.stem: Group consciousness is best described as members' awareness of:
options: The group, its members and what they share
The laws of the host country
questions.explanation: Group consciousness parallels self-consciousness but is directed at the group. Awareness of one's own traits would be self-consciousness.

questions.stem: As a social theory, ethnicity mainly argues against the view that:
options: Conflicts between groups can be reduced
Physical bodies explain differences between people
questions.explanation: Ethnic theory rejects body-based explanations of group difference. The other options are positions it actually supports.

questions.stem: Kasfir (1979) and McCall (1955) are cited for the view that ethnic consciousness:
options: Goes beyond awareness into deliberate affiliations
Is weaker in cities than in villages
questions.explanation: Both stress that ethnic consciousness becomes concrete action and chosen affinities. Nothing in their view makes it genetic.

questions.stem: Group consciousness among migrants is said to become most obvious when they experience:
questions.explanation: Being excluded by the host society pushes migrants together. Full acceptance would weaken the need for a separate group identity.

questions.stem: Students from different Igbo towns, who never mixed at home, form a close union while studying in Moscow and share accommodation tips. This best illustrates:
questions.explanation: Local ties widen into a broader solidarity in a foreign land, creating networks. Assimilation would mean blending into Russian society instead.

questions.stem: The Sabo quarters found in several south-western Nigerian towns are an example of:
options: Geographic and linguistic enclaves formed by migrants
questions.explanation: Sabo settlements are Hausa migrant communities that grew into enclaves with their own trade networks and institutions.

questions.stem: A politician in a cosmopolitan city appoints mostly people from his home area to key posts. Kasfir would see this as ethnic consciousness:
questions.explanation: Kasfir stresses that ethnic consciousness shows itself in deliberate affiliations and action. Here it moves from feeling into choices.

questions.stem: All of the following draw migrants together to create institutions EXCEPT:
options: Solidarity among groups who were not close at home
Ties to a village or region of origin
A sense of commonality in a foreign land
questions.explanation: Controlling extraneous differences is a concern of fair intelligence testing, not a force behind group formation. The rest all bind migrants together.

questions.stem: Which statement about group consciousness in a foreign land is CORRECT?
options: It is only a reaction to nativism
It requires all members to share one village
It also produces trade networks and social institutions
questions.explanation: The course stresses that it is not merely a response to nativism; it builds trade, sociality and enclaves. Members often come from different villages.

questions.stem: In the United States, the application of ethnic theory to race had which unintended result?
options: It reinforced the distinction between whites and blacks
It proved racial differences are genetic
It made ethnicity a purely biological idea
questions.explanation: Although it aimed to downplay the body, it reformulated and reinforced the white-black line. It did not prove genetic differences.

questions.stem: Consider: I. Migrants see each other as compatriots partly because outsiders lump them together. II. Nostalgia for home can bind migrants. III. Group consciousness abroad depends on shared physical ancestry. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and II are both causes given in the course. III is wrong: group consciousness abroad de-emphasises physical ancestry and rests on shared origin and experience.

questions.stem: Which pairing of concept and description is accurate?
options: Ethnic theory: explains differences through physical bodies
Ethnic culture: shared heritage including origin myths, cuisine and dress
Group consciousness: an individual's awareness of personal traits
Ethnic consciousness: a feeling that never shapes action
questions.explanation: Ethnic culture includes heritage, myths, cuisine and dress. Ethnic theory rejects body explanations, and ethnic consciousness does shape action.

questions.stem: A researcher finds that Yoruba and Igbo traders in Accra, rivals in Lagos, form a joint 'Nigerian traders' union' after local hostility. She would most likely conclude that:
options: Ethnic identities are fixed and cannot widen
Exclusion by a host society can widen the circle of solidarity
Ethnic theory has no use outside Nigeria
questions.explanation: Hostility abroad pushed former rivals into a broader national solidarity, showing group boundaries widen under exclusion. Physical similarity plays no part in the explanation.

lesson.title: Are IQ gaps really about genes?
lesson.hook: If a test written in Boston is given to a child in a village near Makurdi, and the child scores low, has the test measured intelligence or measured Boston?

slides.heading: The Bell Curve argument
slides.body:
In 1994, Richard Herrnstein and Charles Murray published **The Bell Curve**. They argued that differences in average IQ scores between ethnic and racial groups are **largely genetic**.

They went further, linking low IQ to social problems such as **low income, unemployment** and poor parenting. In their view, intelligence drove social position, not the other way round.

slides.heading: Why psychologists pushed back
slides.body:
Critics pointed out that **environment** shapes IQ heavily: nutrition, schooling, poverty, language of testing and familiarity with test formats.

The **Flynn effect** showed IQ scores rising across generations in many countries, far too fast for genetic change. An American Psychological Association task force (Neisser and colleagues, 1996) concluded there was no direct evidence for a genetic explanation of group differences in average scores.

slides.question: The authors of The Bell Curve argued that ethnic group differences in IQ are mainly:
slides.why: Herrnstein and Murray claimed a largely genetic basis. Test design and environment are the critics' explanations.

slides.heading: The old mistake in mental testing
slides.body:
Early in the **mental measurement movement**, testers largely ignored ethnic and cultural background. They gave the same tests to everyone and then used the results to rank one ethnic group above others.

The flaw is obvious now. A test built around one culture's words, objects and school habits measures familiarity with that culture as much as raw ability.

slides.heading: The snow question
slides.story: Imagine a test item asking, 'What do you wear when it snows?' Kelechi from Owerri hesitates, not because he cannot reason, but because he has never seen snow. Ask him which rainy-season farm task comes after planting yam and he answers instantly. His classmate from Canada would struggle on that one.
slides.takeaway: Test items carry cultural content, so equal scores require equal familiarity, which is why fairness criteria exist.

slides.heading: Making tests fair today
slides.body:
Modern testing uses specific **criteria for fairness** when one test is used with different ethnic groups. Items are checked for bias, norms are built for each population, and test makers try to **control extraneous differences** such as language, schooling and test experience.

Some tests, like **Raven's Progressive Matrices**, use patterns instead of words to reduce cultural loading, though no test is completely culture-free.

slides.question: When the same test is used across ethnic groups, modern practice tries to control extraneous differences in order to ensure:
slides.why: Fairness criteria aim to make sure scores reflect ability, not language or schooling. Raising scores is not the goal.

slides.heading: Variability within groups
slides.body:
Even where group averages differ, scores **vary widely within every group**. Some members do poorly, many do very well, and the ranges overlap heavily.

This matters: an average tells you almost nothing about the individual in front of you. Judging a student by their group's average is exactly the stereotyping this course warns against.

slides.heading: Why study ethnicity in psychology?
slides.body:
Ethnicity shapes food, language, religion and customs, and through them, how people **see, interpret and respond** to the world. It is also the channel through which culture is **passed on**.

So any psychologist studying perception, motivation, intelligence or mental health must ask how ethnic background shapes the results. Ignoring it, as early testers did, produces misleading science and unfair policies.

slides.heading: How your lecturer will ask this
slides.body: Expect attribution questions on The Bell Curve and essays on why ethnicity matters to research. The trap is presenting Herrnstein and Murray's view as established fact. Present it as a contested claim and give the environmental counter-arguments and fairness criteria.
slides.sampleQuestion: 'Ethnic differences in intelligence scores are essentially genetic.' Critically examine this claim.
slides.howToAnswer: Attribute the claim to Herrnstein and Murray (1994), then counter with environmental factors, the Flynn effect, test bias, fairness criteria and wide within-group variability.

points: The Bell Curve (1994) claimed IQ gaps between groups are largely genetic.
It also linked low IQ to low income, unemployment and poor parenting.
Early testers ignored culture and ranked groups unfairly.
Modern tests use fairness criteria and control extraneous differences.
Scores vary widely within every group, so averages mislead about individuals.

questions.stem: The Bell Curve, which argued for a genetic basis of group IQ differences, was written by:
questions.explanation: Richard Herrnstein and Charles Murray wrote The Bell Curve (1994). Kasfir and McCall wrote on ethnic consciousness.

questions.stem: Modern intelligence testing across ethnic groups uses specific criteria mainly to promote:
questions.explanation: Fairness criteria ensure the same test does not disadvantage some groups. Raising everyone's scores is not their purpose.

questions.stem: Which of the following did The Bell Curve link to low IQ scores?
questions.explanation: Herrnstein and Murray connected low IQ to low income, unemployment and poor parenting. High income is the opposite of their claim.

questions.stem: The main weakness of early mental measurement, as described in the course, was that it:
options: Ignored ethnic background and ranked groups using the same tests
questions.explanation: Early testers disregarded cultural differences and used uniform results to place some groups over others.

questions.stem: The finding that IQ scores in many countries rose substantially over a few generations is known as the:
questions.explanation: The Flynn effect describes rising scores over generations, too fast for genetic change. The Pygmalion effect concerns teacher expectations.

questions.stem: The idea of variability in IQ scores across groups means that:
options: Within each group, some score low while many score high
All members of a group score the same
Group averages predict each person's score
Only one group shows a range of scores
questions.explanation: Every group shows wide variation, so averages say little about individuals. The idea that averages predict individuals is the error it corrects.

questions.stem: A test asks Nigerian pupils to name winter sports, and rural pupils score poorly. A psychologist would most likely say the test is:
questions.explanation: Items tied to unfamiliar cultural content measure exposure, not ability. Treating the result as genetic proof repeats the Bell Curve error.

questions.stem: To reduce language bias when testing children from many Nigerian groups, a researcher would most likely choose a test that:
options: Relies on local proverbs from one group
Uses non-verbal patterns, like Raven's Progressive Matrices
Measures general knowledge of world capitals
questions.explanation: Pattern-based tests reduce dependence on language and specific knowledge. Proverbs from one group would favour that group.

questions.stem: A school head refuses to admit a bright applicant because 'her group scores lower on average'. This decision ignores:
questions.explanation: Wide variation within groups means an average says little about an individual. Using group averages this way is stereotyping.

questions.stem: Which statement about The Bell Curve is CORRECT?
options: It argued that environment fully explains IQ gaps
It was written by the APA task force
It denied any link between IQ and income
It claimed group IQ differences are essentially genetic
questions.explanation: Herrnstein and Murray argued for a largely genetic basis. The APA task force (Neisser et al., 1996) actually found no direct evidence for that view.

questions.stem: 'Controlling extraneous differences' in cross-ethnic testing refers to:
options: Removing low scorers from the sample
Accounting for factors like language and schooling that are not the ability measured
questions.explanation: Extraneous differences are influences other than the ability being tested. Removing low scorers would distort results, not control bias.

questions.stem: The Flynn effect is a problem for a purely genetic account of group IQ differences because:
options: Scores changed too quickly for genes to explain
It occurred only in one ethnic group
It proves tests are perfectly fair
questions.explanation: Large gains within a few generations point to environmental causes, since gene pools change slowly. It does not show IQ is fixed.

questions.stem: Consider: I. The Bell Curve linked low IQ to poor parental behaviour. II. Early testers carefully adjusted for culture. III. Modern fairness criteria apply when the same test is used across groups. Which are correct?
questions.explanation: I and III are correct. II is false: early mental measurement ignored ethnic differences, which is why fairness criteria were later developed.

questions.stem: Which pairing of name and idea is accurate?
options: Flynn: IQ gaps are fixed by genes
Neisser et al. (1996): no direct evidence for a genetic explanation of group differences
Herrnstein and Murray: tests are always culture-free
questions.explanation: The APA task force led by Neisser found no direct support for genetic explanations of group gaps. Flynn's work points the other way, towards environment.

questions.stem: A study finds that urban and rural children of the same ethnic group differ more in test scores than urban children of two different ethnic groups. This most strongly supports the view that:
options: Rural children are less intelligent by nature
Tests should only be given in cities
questions.explanation: If setting matters more than ethnicity, environment (schooling, exposure) is the stronger influence. Calling rural children naturally less intelligent ignores that conclusion.
